newsitem.title: GERMANY: Economy worries prompt Germans to cut back on beer.
newsitem.headline: Economy worries prompt Germans to cut back on beer.

text.p: Germans, worried about their country's struggling economy and their own health, are cutting down on their beloved beer and switching to alcohol-free drinks, German brewers said on Monday.

The German Brewers' Association (DBB) President Michael Dietzsch said annual per capita beer consumption dropped by 4.2 litres to 131.7 litres in 1996 and German beer production fell over 200 million litres to 11.4 billion litres.

Dietzsch told a news conference economic reasons such as falling real income, high unemployment and consumer uncertainty over government plans for tax and pension reforms were pushing Germans to cut back on their favourite brew.
He also said last year's wet summer, health concerns and the debate about alcohol abuse had contributed to the decline.

The average German drank one crate, or 10 litres, less beer in 1996 than in 1991. Employment in the sector fell by a third to 46,500 between 1991 and 1996 and the number of breweries fell by 122 to 1,234.
Dietzsch said although the country was still the world's third largest beer producer, behind the United States and China, closures and job losses in the industry would continue.

But he said Germany would stay one of the world's biggest beer markets, making it a takeover target for foreign firms, although the fragmented nature of the market and the small size of many German breweries could deter potential buyers.
